en: Verses on the Refutation of Objections (Vigrahavyāvartanī-kārikā)
If no intrinsic nature (svabhāva) exists for any entities whatsoever,

then your statement, being itself devoid of intrinsic nature, is not capable of negating intrinsic nature. Alternatively, if this statement possesses intrinsic nature, then your previous thesis is destroyed.
In that case, you must state both the reason for the inequality and the specific cause [for your position].
Your thought might be, "It is like the word 'not'"; however, this is not tenable, for here the existing word "not" serves to exclude the future [word].
If you think that the negation of the negation is likewise [invalid], that too is incorrect.
In this way, it is your thesis that is refuted according to its definition, not mine.
For if you first perceive entities through direct perception and then seek to negate them, [you contradict yourself].
Therefore, there is no perception by which entities are apprehended.
Inference has already been refuted along with perception, scripture, and analogy;
as have those objects established by inference and scripture, and those established by examples.

And those who know the states of wholesome phenomena consider the wholesome to be their intrinsic nature; this same application [of the term] applies to the remaining cases as well. Those phenomena which have the nature of leading to liberation, and those which lead to liberation—[of these...]
Thus, for those very states of phenomena such as "not leading to liberation" and so forth that have been described:
if there were no intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of phenomena, then even the name "absence of intrinsic nature" (niḥsvabhāva) would not exist;
for indeed, a name does not exist without a referent (nirvastuka).
Now, if intrinsic nature exists, yet it does not exist in phenomena,
then it is logical to teach that which possesses that intrinsic nature as being without phenomena.
For negation applies only to what exists, as in the case [of the statement], "There is no jar in the house."
Therefore, this negation of an existing intrinsic nature has been observed by you.
Now, if that intrinsic nature does not exist, what indeed is being negated by you with this speech? For the negation of a non-existent thing is established even without speech.
Just as children falsely perceive water in a mirage, so too would there be a false apprehension on your part regarding that which is being negated because it does not exist. [Objection:
But if this is so, then there exists an apprehension, an object of apprehension, and an apprehender.
The negation, the object of negation, and the negator— these constitute that group of six.
Now, if there is neither grasping, nor the object of grasping,
nor graspers, then surely the negation, the object of negation, and the negators do exist?
If the negation, the object to be negated, and the negator do not exist, then all things are established, as is their very nature.
Furthermore, since they lack intrinsic nature, your reason is not established; for from where could your reason come?
Furthermore, the establishment of this matter of yours [the self] as being without cause is not tenable.
(NagVvy 17) If, for you, the establishment of the cessation of intrinsic nature occurs without a cause, then for me too, the existence of intrinsic nature is established without a cause. (NagVvy 18)
Furthermore, it is untenable that the existence of a cause implies the lack of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatva) in things;
for in the world, there is no entity whatsoever that is devoid of intrinsic nature.
Moreover, it is untenable that the negation comes first and the object of negation comes later.

Since my word is not established either subsequently, nor simultaneously, because it possesses an intrinsic nature [only when] in the presence of the totality of causes and conditions, or even separately; if that is so,
then emptiness is established for all things, because they lack an intrinsic nature.
That which is the dependent existence of things is declared to be emptiness;
for that which exists dependently indeed lacks intrinsic nature.
A magical creation [created] by a magical creation, or a person of illusion created by one's own magic—
Just as one might negate [an object], so too would this negation be.
This statement is not possessed of intrinsic nature; therefore, there is no loss of my position.
Nor is there any inconsistency, and no special reason need be stated.
"Let there be no sound"—this example which you have undertaken is not valid;
for by means of a sound, that very sound is warded off, but this case is not like that.
If, indeed, the warding off of things devoid of intrinsic nature were itself accomplished by means of something devoid of intrinsic nature, [then your objection would hold].

For if the absence of intrinsic nature were to cease, intrinsic nature itself would necessarily be established. Or rather, just as one might have the false apprehension that there is a woman in a magically created woman, so too might this occur for someone regarding a magical creation. (NagVvy 26–27)

Alternatively, this reason is "equal to the probandum" (sādhyasama), for there is no existence of sound [as a real entity]. Furthermore, we do not speak without relying upon conventional usage (saṃvyavahāra).
If I had any thesis (pratijñā) whatsoever, then this fault would be mine.

I have no thesis; therefore, I am not at fault. If I were to perceive anything, I would either affirm or deny it by means of objects such as direct perception; since that [perception] does not exist for me, I am beyond reproach.

And if those various objects are established for you by means of valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*), then tell me: how are those very valid cognitions themselves established? If the establishment of valid cognitions were to occur through other valid cognitions, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Therein, there is no establishment of the beginning, nor indeed of the middle, nor of the end.
Furthermore, if their establishment occurs without means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), your argument is abandoned;
in that case, there would be an inconsistency, and you must state the specific reason for it.
This is an unequal comparison; for fire does not illuminate itself.
Indeed, its non-perception is never observed, as is the case with a jar in the dark.
And if this fire illuminates itself according to your statement, [then...]
Indeed, fire would burn its own self as if it were another;
for if fire illuminates both itself and others by means of your statement,
then darkness would conceal both itself and others, just like fire.
There is no darkness in fire, nor where that supreme self, the fire, resides.
How could it produce illumination? For illumination is the destruction of darkness.
To claim that "fire illuminates at the very moment it arises" is an untenable doctrine.
For fire does not reach the darkness even as it is arising.
Alternatively, if fire were to destroy darkness without reaching it,
then this fire situated here would destroy the darkness in all world-systems.

If, for you, the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) occurs by itself without depending on the objects of cognition (*prameya*), then the establishment of the means of valid cognition is independent; this is what is meant by "establishment by itself" (*svataḥsiddhi*).
For if your establishment of the means of valid cognition were without depending on the objects of cognition, [then it would be established by itself].
These means of valid cognition do not belong to anyone in this way.
Now, if it is thought that their establishment is dependent [on something else], what fault is there in that?
There would be the proof of what is already established; for that which is not yet established does not depend on another.
For if the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were established in every respect only by depending upon the objects of cognition (*prameya*),
then the establishment of the objects of cognition would not occur by depending on the means of valid cognition at all.
And if the establishment of the objects of cognition occurs without depending on the means of valid cognition, [then they are established independently].

What is the use of establishing the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)? Those very things for whose sake they are established are already well-known. But if, on the other hand, the establishment of your means of valid cognition depends upon the objects of cognition (prameya), then in that case, the relationship between the means of valid cognition and the objects of cognition is certainly reversed.
Now, if for you the establishment of the objects of cognition depends on the establishment of the means of cognition,
and the establishment of the means of cognition depends on the establishment of the objects of cognition, then there is no establishment of either for you.
For if the objects of cognition were established by those very means of cognition, [the same would apply to the means].
And how will those [means of valid cognition], which are themselves to be established by the objects of cognition, establish them?
If those means of valid cognition are established by the very objects of cognition,
then how will those objects of cognition be established by those [means of valid cognition]?

If a son is to be produced by a father, and that very son is likewise to produce a father—if this were so, tell me, who would produce whom? Furthermore, in that case, who is the father and who is the son? You yourself must explain both of these.

Since we possess the characteristics of father and son, there is no doubt in this matter. (NagVvy 50) The establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not occur through themselves, nor through one another, nor through other means of valid cognition;
it does not occur through the objects of cognition (*prameya*), nor indeed without a cause. (NagVvy 51)
Those who know the state of phenomena would say that the wholesome nature of wholesome dharmas should be expressed through such a distinction;
for if a wholesome intrinsic nature arises dependently, it belongs to the wholesome [dharmas].
If the other-nature of phenomena is indeed their own-nature, how can this be?
(53) Alternatively, if an own-nature arises without depending on anything at all, then for wholesome phenomena there would be no abiding in the holy life. (54)
There would be neither non-dharma nor dharma, nor would there be worldly conventions;
furthermore, things possessing intrinsic nature would be eternal, because they would be eternal by virtue of being causeless.
Thus, the same fault applies to unwholesome states, neutral states, and those conducive to liberation, and so forth.

Therefore, for you, everything—both the conditioned and the unconditioned—becomes real indeed. If someone here were to say that whatever has a name exists as having intrinsic nature (sasvabhāva), you should reply to him: "We do not say that names are real. (NagVvy 56–57)
Regarding this statement "name is non-existent," does it belong to that which exists or to that which does not exist?
For whether it belongs to the existent or to the non-existent, in both cases your argument fails.
Furthermore, the emptiness of all entities has already been established previously.

Therefore, this constitutes a censure of that [position], and this is also a refutation of the lack of a formal thesis. Furthermore, as for the doubt expressed in the statement, "If intrinsic nature exists, yet it does not exist in phenomena," that too has been rendered free from doubt.
If emptiness is the negation of that which exists, then surely this is well-established;
for you are indeed negating the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) of entities. But if you negate emptiness itself, then that emptiness does not exist.

If you say that there is a negation of an existent, then this very position of yours is abandoned. I do not negate anything, nor is there anything to be negated; therefore, when you say "you negate," you are merely leveling a false accusation against me.

And as for the claim that the establishment of a negation statement occurs because of a word that does not apprehend [a real object], in this case, the statement "speech is non-existent" merely makes it known; it does not negate it.
Furthermore, regarding the great discussion you have raised concerning the example of the mirage:
In this regard, hear the definitive conclusion as to how that illustration is logically established:
If that grasping were to exist by way of its own intrinsic nature (svabhāva), it would not have arisen dependently.
And that which arises dependently—surely that very grasping is emptiness (śūnyatā).
If grasping existed by way of intrinsic nature, who could turn back that grasping?
Know that this same [logic] applies to the remaining [categories] as well; therefore, this is not a valid objection.
By this, the absence of a reason has already been answered previously, because of their equality.
That reason which was previously stated in the refutation of the analogy of the mirage,
and which has already been answered regarding the three times due to its symmetry,
becomes a counter-reason for the proponents of emptiness across the three times.
For whom this emptiness prevails, for them all goals prevail;
for whom emptiness does not prevail, nothing at all prevails.
[He who understands] emptiness, dependent origination, and the middle way—
I bow to that one of incomparable intelligence, who has taught [all things] as having a single meaning.
